case_name: Makow v. Winnipeg Sun et al.

IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF MANITOBA

March 30, 2004

PER CURIAM

The defendants (the
Sun) were held liable in a defamation suit initiated by the plaintiff (Dr.
Makow) as a result of an article published in
The Winnipeg Sun
paper on
June 17, 2000.  The damages were assessed at $5,000.

The Sun appeals the
judgment against it, and Dr. Makow cross-appeals with respect to the award of
damages.

The learned trial
judge provided lengthy reasons for decision, including a careful review of the
evidence.  He made findings of fact based upon the credibility of witnesses.
He reviewed the offending article in a meticulous manner, separating those
portions which were supported by evidence, and therefore justified, from
portions for which he concluded there was no justification.  He also considered
the possible defence of fair comment and ruled that it had no application given
the circumstances of the case and his findings of fact.

On this appeal, the
primary thrust of the Sun’s submission is that the trial judge fell into error
in segmenting the offending article into small components rather than taking a
broad look at the article in its entirety and then determining the gist or
sting of the publication.  Had this process been followed, it is argued, the
court would have or should have found the article to be justified as being
substantially true and as fair comment on a matter of public interest.

It is not our purpose
to repeat the background facts with the same detail as the learned trial
judge.  It will be sufficient to indicate that Dr. Makow was engaged as a
stipendiary lecturer at the University of Winnipeg during the academic year
1999/2000.  Without meaning to make a precise finding on the matter, it would
seem that a stipendiary lecturer is roughly equivalent to a person serving at
the pleasure of the University.  His employment was not renewed.  We are
informed that there is ongoing litigation between Dr. Makow and the University
of Winnipeg.  What is clear is that Dr. Makow is of the belief that the
non-renewal of his stipendiary status has to do with his views on the
“feminist” culture, whereas the University holds a different view.

The conflict between
Dr. Makow and the University of Winnipeg preceded the publication of the
article leading to this defamation action.  The conflict came to the attention
of local newspapers in Winnipeg and resulted in an article in
The Winnipeg
Sun
commenting favourably on Dr. Makow and his problems at the
University.  The article was written by Michael Coren and published in the
final edition on Thursday, June 15, 2000, in the section dealing with
“opinions.”  In that article, the author becomes the mouthpiece for Dr. Makow,
explaining that he is being ousted by the University because of complaints
raised by a small group of feminist radicals in his class and an unsympathetic
administration.  The article suggests that Dr. Makow is victimized by feminine
zealots waging a campaign against him because he is not a radical feminist and
is a heterosexual.

Two days later,
The
Winnipeg Sun
published an article in the opinion section of the paper by
Lyn Cockburn under a title “Stow your sympathy for ‘maligned’ prof.”  In preparing
the article, Ms Cockburn interviewed one member of the class who was highly
critical of Dr. Makow.  The offending article reads as follows:

You read
Michael Coren’s column Thursday so you’re all sympathied up over the plight of
poor Henry Makow who (sob) says he lost his job as an English prof at the U of
W because:  he’s not a radical feminist, is heterosexual, defends marriage,
believes men are not women’s enemies and was the victim of an anonymous letter
written by four radicals in one of his classes.

I don’t
know how old Michael’s children are but I suspect he would not want an
18-year-old daughter of his present in a first year English class taught by a
50-year-old man who announced one day he had beaten his ex-girlfriend (“she
started it”) and afterwards they “had great makeup sex.”

It seems
Michael was so busy quoting poor Henry Makow he forgot to talk to any of the
18-year-old daughters who listened to the prof day after day.

I sat
down with one of those daughters Thursday morning, and the first thing she said
to me was, “This has nothing to do with feminism.  He’s blown this up into
something about feminism.  It’s about unprofessional conduct.”

But when
I contacted Makow he said, “That’s ridiculous.  This is the way feminists
censure people they don’t agree with.”

And just
how unprofessional was Mr. Makow’s conduct?

Depends
on what you think your daughter (or son) should have to listen to in a
first-year English course.

Do you
want your daughter asked in class and out of class (Makow questioned young
women outside the classroom) when and how she lost her innocence?

Would you
like her to be told that women should devote their lives to serving their men
because the high divorce rate in North America is caused by women who have
careers and are not therefore good mothers.  (During a telephone conversation,
Makow said to me:  “The university has an agenda to encourage women to pursue
careers and not follow the more traditional path.”)

Would you
like your daughter to be asked in class, and again outside class, if a certain
passage in a D.H. Lawrence novel aroused her?

Want her
subjected to the statement that religious Jews and Muslims look ridiculous
because of the way they dress?

Want her
in a class where the professor shouts at his students?  Do you want her asked
in class and out for details about her relationship with her boyfriend, if she
happens to have one?  Or in a class where the professor talks about his sex
life?

And for
those readers whose sympathies still lie with Makow, may I point out that much
of what Makow said in class is on tape.  And everything he said was witnessed
by enough students to resink the
Titanic
.

Makow
himself says, “Everything I said in class had a definite academic purpose.”

The young
woman I interviewed is on tape saying to Makow:  “You’re in a position of
authority.  It’s not like you’re my friend asking me these kinds of questions.
You’re the professor.”

Makow
says everything he said got twisted.  “It’s all a distortion.”  The young woman
I interviewed Thursday morning said it is Makow who twisted the situation.

“Personal
information is not appropriate for a classroom,” she said.

And why
have I not named her?  Because she’s afraid.  So are the other women (a total
of 11 young women instituted the initial complaint against Makow and they did
so with the approval and knowledge of the majority of their classmates) who
also do not want their names used.

“We have
reason to be scared of him,” said the young woman, adding that she and her
friends were indeed worried when Makow talked about beating his ex-girlfriend
(even if it was her fault!).

Nonetheless,
the official letter of complaint was not anonymous.  Seven young women signed
it.  The signature of the young woman I interviewed is on that letter.

It is a
letter which complains about Makow’s inappropriate comments and questions,
about his conduct, his yelling at students in class.

I brought
up Makow’s accusation that “gender feminists are waging a campaign against
heterosexuality” and the young woman sitting across from me shook her head and
threw up her hands.  She repeated the statement that the complaint didn’t have
anything to do with feminism in the first place and said that heterosexuality
had absolutely nothing to do with the incident.

I have a
daughter, Michael Coren, and after the family doctor made inappropriate remarks
and gestures to her, I wanted him disbarred or whatever the hell it is that is
done with doctors.

I would
feel the same way about a professor who made inappropriate unprofessional
remarks to my daughter, in or out of class.

I think
most parents would feel exactly the same.

Poor,
poor Henry.  Silly, silly Michael.

A statement of claim
was filed on July 26, 2000, asserting that the article was understood to mean
that Dr. Makow was “irresponsible, immoral, bigoted, dishonest, intimidating
and incompetent” and unfit to retain his position as a lecturer.  It was
asserted that the article contained 12 statements which were defamatory of Dr.
Makow.

The Sun defended the
action on the basis of truth and, where opinions were expressed, on fair
comment.

Dr. Makow testified on
his own behalf.  A number of students were called as witnesses for the
plaintiff, and the thrust of their evidence was that his lectures and his
conduct generally were acceptable.  Defence witnesses generally supported the
views expressed in the article by Ms Cockburn.  As has been noted, the
process followed by the learned trial judge was to dissect the article, almost
on a sentence-by-sentence basis, weigh the competing evidence on the matter and
then make a finding as to whether the Sun had established the truth of that
particular assertion.  The learned trial judge found that many of the
statements of fact had been established.  However, he specifically found that
the Sun had failed to justify the following four statements:

(1)     that he had asked a young
woman, out of class, when and how she had lost her innocence;

(2)     that he had inquired of a
student, in and out of class, as to whether she had been aroused by a
particular passage in a novel;

(3)     that he would have alleged
that religious Jews and Muslims look ridiculous because of the way they dress;
and

(4)     that he would have
intimidated students.

Concerning the defence
of fair comment, the learned trial judge concluded that the opinions expressed
by Ms Cockburn towards the end of the article, where it is implied that Dr.
Makow is to be compared with a lascivious physician, could not fall within the
defence of fair comment since they were “predicated upon statements which have
not been proven to be true and must, therefore, be assumed as false” (at para.
126).

As has been noted, the
thrust of this appeal is that the sting of the article is to be found by
reading the article in its entirety.  It is argued that the sting or gist of
the article is that Dr. Makow was “unfit to be a teacher by virtue of conduct
in which he shouted at, or intimidated students, asked about personal lives,
discussed his sex life in class while at the same time linking it to acts of
violence, and discussed arousal in a sexual context with a youthful student.”
It is argued that there was evidence which the court found to be credible which
supported these assertions and that it was fair comment to contend that Dr.
Makow was unfit.

We cannot accept this
submission.

While the approach is
not precisely the same as that of the learned trial judge, the court arrives at
the same conclusion.

It is our view that
the most damaging assertions in the article are those that suggest that Dr.
Makow pursued discussions out of class with individual students concerning
sexual issues.  These assertions were not established by the evidence.
Moreover, the assertions were linked with the suggestion that Dr. Makow is
comparable to a salacious physician acting inappropriately with a young patient.

The learned trial
judge found that there had been classroom discussion about the loss of
innocence, which arose during a discussion of the novel
Settlers of the
Marsh
.  During the course of that discussion, one class member was
embarrassed by being asked when she had lost her innocence – meaning her
virginity.  But the learned trial judge found that there was no evidence to
support the suggestion that this line of questioning had been pursued with any
student outside the classroom.

Similarly, there was classroom
discussion about
Lady Chatterley’s Lover
by D. H. Lawrence, and Dr.
Makow raised the question of whether the students were aroused.  But again, the
damaging assertion is that the subject was pursued out of class with a student
or students on an individual basis.  The learned trial judge found no evidence
to support that assertion.

The implication to be
taken from the article is that Dr. Makow may be some kind of sexual predator
ready to take advantage of his young female students.  That implication is made
real when linked with the comparison of Dr. Makow, the professor who made
inappropriate, unprofessional remarks in and out of class, with a family doctor
making inappropriate remarks and gestures to a young female patient during the
course of a medical examination.

Concerning the defence
of justification, both facts and opinions can be justified, but only if the
facts are substantially true and the statements of opinion are correct on a
true view of the state of events as disclosed by the facts (as opposed to just
being fair). See
Gatley on Libel and Slander
[1]
.

Thus, the statements
of fact must be proven to be substantially true in their material allegations,
not only in their literal meaning, but also in any inferential or innuendo
meaning the statements may be found to bear.  It is the sting on the main
charge of the libel that must be proven to be true.  See, for example,
Hodgson
v. Canadian Newspapers Co.
[2]

and
Sidorsky v. CFCN Communications Ltd.
[3]

We agree with the
trial judge that the defence of justification is not available where, as here,
certain important allegations were not established and where the innuendo
flowing from those statements was not proven to be true.  The defence of
justification therefore fails.

With respect to the
defence of fair comment, it will only be successful if the comment is based
upon facts which have been proven to be true.  “… [T]he essence of a plea of
fair comment is that the facts underlying it are true”:
Pressler v.
Lethbridge
[4]
.

Some question has
arisen in the cases as to whether in the defence of fair comment, the
underlying facts must be established with the same degree of completeness as in
the defence of justification.  For example, there are some decisions of the Manitoba
trial court which take the view that the defendant must prove that each and
every statement of fact upon which the comment is based is true.  See, for
example,
Maloney v. Winnipeg Free Press Co. Ltd. et al.
[5]

and
Pearlman v. Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and Carlyle-Gorge
[6]
.

This court agrees and
adopts a more lenient standard which is in accord with most jurisdictions in
Canada to the effect that it is the material and essential facts upon which the
comment is based that must be proved to be substantially true.  A defence of
fair comment will not lie if there has been a misstatement of a material fact.
As stated by Lord Denning M.R. in
London Artists Ltd. v. Littler
[7]

(at p. 391):

In order
to be fair, the commentator must get his basic facts right.  The basic facts
are those which go to the pith and substance of the matter:  ….

See, for example,
Leenen v. Canadian Broadcasting Corp.
[8]
,

Burnett et al. v. Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and MacIntyre (No. 1)
[9]

and
Ross v.
New Brunswick
Teachers’ Assn
.
[10]

In this case, there
has been misstatement of material facts.  Fair comment cannot constitute a
defence to the unsupported suggestion that Dr. Makow is a sexual predator.

We now turn to the
cross-appeal on damages.

In arriving at his
award of $5,000 damages, the learned trial judge took into account the fact
that Dr. Makow’s reputation was already diminished to some degree by virtue of
his conduct in the classroom.  That is to say, there was validity to almost all
of the allegations against him relative to what occurred within the classroom.

Dr. Makow advanced no
claim for special or consequential damages.

The learned trial
judge also found that the article was published without malice.  In our view,
that conclusion is supported by evidence and should not be disturbed on
appellate review.  Moreover, it was Dr. Makow himself who elected to use the
pages of
The Winnipeg Sun
for his own purposes in setting forth his
position in his dispute with the University in the most favourable light.  It
is understandable that there should be a response showing another aspect of the
matter.  While the article should have been framed more carefully, its
publication was an attempt to provide balance rather than to do injury.

In summary, we would
dismiss both the appeal by the Sun with respect to liability and the appeal by
Dr. Makow regarding damages.

Since Dr. Makow
enjoyed substantial success on appeal, he is entitled to costs in this court.
